name: Bonemass maximising

lead: Bonemass maximising is a looksmaxxing term for deliberately building bone mass, the amount and density of mineralised bone, in the hope of a more robust facial skeleton and body frame. Forum guides present bone as living tissue that responds to nutrition, mechanical load, hormones and sleep, and treat childhood and the teens as the key window for reaching peak bone mass.

The appearance chain proposed is: more bone laid down during growth, then thicker cheekbones, jaw and wrists and a more developed frame. Research on bone mass supports the general science of how diet, calcium and loading affect bone and when peak bone mass is reached, but studies measuring visible facial change in healthy people from these habits have not been published.

paras: Guides typically combine a calcium- and protein-adequate diet, vitamin D and vitamin K discussions, resistance and impact training, sleep, and avoidance of smoking and heavy alcohol. Younger members are told the earlier the better, because bone mass accrues most during puberty. Some threads add supplement lists called stacks, and some separate threads discuss prescription drugs or peptides; those are described only as a topic of discussion here.

Diet and exercise elements carry the usual considerations of those habits, such as excess supplemental calcium or vitamin D, which clinicians advise taking only as recommended. The prescription drugs and research peptides mentioned in some guides carry their own side effects and legal restrictions, and several are used in osteoporosis care under medical supervision. Ageing and growth plates set limits on what changes in adulthood.

angle.text: Proponents use bone mass as the foundation for a stronger-looking jaw, cheekbones and frame. The routes people describe are diet, resistance and impact training and sleep, with the biggest emphasis on the teenage years.

lead: Bonemass maximising, often written as bone mass or bonemass, is a practice and discussion topic in looksmaxxing communities about increasing the quantity and density of bone through lifestyle. A widely shared looksmax.org guide describes bone as a living tissue that responds to nutrition, physical activity, hormones, sleep and lifestyle, and argues that genetics play a large part but do not firmly limit potential.[1]

The appearance motivation is that bone mass affects facial structure and body proportions: proponents link it to cheekbone and jaw robustness, brow ridges and wrist and shoulder width.[1] Guides stress that growth and peak bone mass during childhood and puberty are the key period, and describe adulthood as a time of modelling in response to mechanical stress and maintenance.[1]

In the medical literature, peak bone mass is the maximum amount of bone reached in life, typically in the early twenties for women and late twenties for men according to encyclopedic summaries.[2] Reviews of bone modelling and remodelling describe the cellular processes involved, and trials in children have studied calcium supplementation and bone mineral gain.[3][4]

paras: Bone mass in the medical sense is the amount of mineralised bone tissue, usually assessed by size and bone mineral density.[2][5] In looksmaxxing usage it also stands for visible skeletal robustness. Guides distinguish bone growth in length, which they say ends with the growth plates, from thickening and density, which they say continue to respond to stress in adulthood.[1]

Threads range from long guides for beginners, to requests for help with a stack, to threads aimed at teens, to discussions of drugs-only approaches and arguments between members over whether sugar-heavy diets or other methods matter.[6][7][8]

Proponents hold that bone responds to mechanical stress and that heavy lifting, impact and chewing-related loading encourage deposition. They also point to nutrition, noting calcium, vitamin D and protein, and to hormones and sleep as influences.[1] Some members claim that gains are available at any stage of development, while others restrict the idea to puberty.[9]
Several threads emphasise puberty as the stage when the skeleton is most responsive, arguing that habits adopted early have the largest effect on final structure.[1][10]

Reviews describe bone as constantly remodelled, with formation and resorption controlled by cell signalling pathways and hormones, which is the biological basis for the idea that bone can respond to its environment.[3] A randomised trial in prepubertal girls found that calcium supplementation led to greater bone mineral gain that was still partly present years after supplementation stopped.[4]

Researchers working on skeletal health focus on bone density and fracture risk, not on facial appearance, and published studies of facial bone shape change in healthy people through diet or exercise have not been located. Public summaries note that peak bone mass is reached in early adulthood and that puberty strongly affects bone size.[2]

Guides that move into drugs and peptides raise the general risks of those substances. Medical literature on drugs that act on bone, such as parathyroid hormone preparations and bisphosphonates, concerns supervised treatment of osteoporosis.[11][12] Nutrients taken above recommended levels can cause problems, and clinicians generally advise following recommended intakes.

No studies found on bonemass maximising as a looksmaxxing practice. Related research on bone mass includes a randomised trial of calcium supplementation in prepubertal girls,[4] a trial of parathyroid hormone in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis,[11] and a trial of etidronate in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis,[12] which concern bone density and fractures and not facial appearance.
